## The idea

Two performances can share every written pitch and duration yet seem to describe
different gestures. One clips each note at half its allotted time. Another lets
notes overlap, leans into the high point, and delays the next arrival by a small
amount. The score establishes events; performance determines how those events
occupy the air.

*Articulation* describes how notes connect or separate. Dynamics shape amplitude
over time, while phrasing uses accent, timing, and contour to group events into
larger motions. The distinction is clearest when the event data remains strict
and several renderers interpret it. Expressive choices then stay visible
as policies instead of becoming unexplained edits to the score.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 82
use_synth :piano

score = [
  {note: :c4, start: 0, duration: 1},
  {note: :d4, start: 1, duration: 1},
  {note: :e4, start: 2, duration: 1},
  {note: :g4, start: 3, duration: 2},
  {note: :e4, start: 5, duration: 1},
  {note: :d4, start: 6, duration: 1},
  {note: :c4, start: 7, duration: 2}
]

define :play_events do |events, shaped|
  cursor = 0
  events.each_with_index do |event, index|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    high_point = event[:note] == :g4
    amp = shaped ? (0.55 + index * 0.05 + (high_point ? 0.2 : 0)) : 0.7
    ratio = shaped ? (high_point ? 1.05 : 0.82) : 0.5
    offset = shaped && index == 4 ? 0.08 : 0
    sleep offset
    play event[:note], sustain: event[:duration] * ratio,
      release: 0.08, amp: amp
    sleep event[:duration] - offset
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

play_events score, false
sleep 2
play_events score, true
```

The first renderer treats every event alike: equal amplitude and a sound lasting
half of its nominal slot. The second grows toward G, allows that high point to
last, and delays the following E slightly. Both performances read the same pitch
and score-time values. Listen for a change in grouping rather than a change in
the tune itself.

## Change one thing

1. Set the strict ratio to `1.05`. Each sounding note now extends past the next
   onset, producing legato overlap without changing a single event in `score`.
2. Move the accent from G to the final C. The phrase now gives its greatest
   amplitude to the arrival rather than to the melodic high point. Notice how
   that shifts the perceived goal.
3. Increase the offset from `0.08` to `0.3`. A small hesitation becomes a
   conspicuous delay, and because the event must still fit its score slot, the
   time left for sounding is reduced.

## Why it works

Every score event follows the shared schema `:note`, `:start`, and `:duration`.
Start identifies an onset on the metric timeline, while duration reserves a
slot. The renderer decides how much of that slot actually sounds and at what
amplitude. Staccato can therefore shorten a note without corrupting the bar
total or moving the next written onset.

Expression becomes a mapping from structural events to playback parameters.
The high-point rule derives emphasis from pitch; the crescendo derives it from
position in the phrase; the offset singles out one arrival. Each policy can be
replaced or combined without editing the source notes, which makes disagreements
about performance concrete enough to inspect.

A quantised rendering may sound rigid, but useful deviation depends on musical
style and on the scale of the gesture. The two passes provide an audible
comparison, not a proof that the shaped one is superior. Ruby can validate the
program, but only listening on the intended system can reveal whether an
eight-hundredths-of-a-beat offset is perceptible or whether the amplitude curve feels
misplaced.

Amplitude is relative. Raising every event to `0.9` makes the phrase louder but
does not create a high point. A crescendo suggests direction because successive
values form a slope; an accent creates a local contrast with its neighbours.
The policies can assign the same numeric amplitude to one note while producing
different phrase shapes around it.

This renderer sleeps through each full event slot, so a positive onset offset
reduces the available sounding time. Another design could preserve the note's
duration and push all later onsets, changing the complete timeline. Once score
time and performance time have separate variables, neither choice has to remain
implicit. Name the renderer or its fields so the selected timing policy can be
understood without reverse-engineering the sleeps.

## Take it further

Add optional `:amp` and `:articulation` fields to selected events. Teach
`play_events` to interpret `:staccato`, `:legato`, and `:accent`, falling back
to renderer defaults when a field is absent. Produce detached, fully legato,
and phrase-shaped performances from the same score. Keep every pitch, start, and
duration unchanged, then compare the renderers by the kinds of connection and
emphasis they produce.
